justifications.decision: yadvat/tadvat is rendered as the correlative “as/so,” with samudram as the object of the first praviśanti and yam puruṣam as the object of the second.
options_considered: Take the first praviśanti literally of waters entering the ocean and the second of desires entering a person.
Take both clauses as describing only physical inflow into the ocean.
Take yam as referring back to samudram rather than to a person.
justifications.chosen: The first half is an ocean simile: waters enter an ocean that is being filled yet remains unmoved; the second half applies this to desires entering a person.

evidence.quote: samudram āpaḥ sarvato gatāḥ praviśanti svātmastham avikriyam eva santaṃ yadvat, tadvat kāmāḥ ... yaṃ puruṣam --- samudram iva āpaḥ -- ... praviśanti
evidence.translation: “As waters, come from all sides, enter the ocean, which remains established in itself and unchanged, so desires enter that person—like waters the ocean.”

justifications.decision: I render it “fixed in unmoving stability,” qualifying samudram.
justifications.chosen: acala-pratiṣṭham is a bahuvrīhi: “whose stability/abiding is unmoving,” not a separate adjective plus noun and not “founded on a mountain.”

evidence.quote: acala-pratiṣṭham acalatayā pratiṣṭhā avasthitiḥ yasya tam acala-pratiṣṭhaṃ
evidence.translation: “acala-pratiṣṭha: that whose pratiṣṭhā, abiding/stability, is by immovability.”

justifications.decision: I do not translate the clause as indulgence or satisfaction of desires; I render it as desires entering/dissolving without unsettling him.
options_considered: Desires enter him by being absorbed without perturbation.
Desires enter him as temptations that overpower him.
Desires enter him because he actively pursues and enjoys them.
justifications.chosen: The kāmāḥ that enter the person are particular desires arising even amid sense-objects; their “entering” means dissolving in the self without disturbing or enslaving him.

evidence.quote: kāmāḥ viṣaya-saṃnidhāv api sarvataḥ icchā-viśeṣāḥ yaṃ puruṣam ... avikurvantaḥ praviśanti sarve ātmany eva pralīyante na svātma-vaśaṃ kurvanti
evidence.translation: “The desires—particular wishes from all sides, even in the presence of sense-objects—enter that person without altering him; all dissolve in the self and do not bring him under their control.”

justifications.decision: I translate śāntim āpnoti as “he attains peace—liberation.” The bhāṣya plaintext reads śāntir mokṣam, apparently an unproofread form for śāntiṃ/mokṣam; I cite it only for the explicit śānti = mokṣa gloss.
options_considered: śānti as only ordinary calm or quietude.
justifications.chosen: śāntim means not merely psychological calm but liberation (mokṣa) in Śaṅkara’s gloss.

justifications.decision: I render na kāma-kāmī as “not the craver of objects of desire,” not as “not one who desires desires.”
options_considered: kāma-kāmī as “one who craves objects of desire,” Śaṅkara’s interpretation.
kāma-kāmī as the awkward literal “one who desires desires.”
kāma-kāmī as simply “a sensual man,” without preserving the compound’s object relation.
justifications.chosen: kāma-kāmī is the person who habitually desires objects of desire; he does not attain peace/liberation.

evidence.quote: netaraḥ kāma-kāmī, kāmyanta iti kāmāḥ viṣayāḥ tān kāmayituṃ śīlaṃ yasya saḥ kāma-kāmī, naiva prāpnotīty arthaḥ
evidence.translation: “Not the other, the kāma-kāmī: kāmāḥ are objects, because they are desired; one whose habit is to desire them is a kāma-kāmī. The meaning is: he certainly does not attain it.”

translation:
As waters enter the ocean,
which is being filled yet fixed in unmoving stability,
so all desires enter that man, all of them—
dissolving in himself without unsettling him.
He attains peace, liberation (śānti);
not the craver of objects of desire (kāma-kāmī).
one_shot_delta: A commentary-blind translation might take kāma-kāmī as “one who desires desires”; Śaṅkara instead defines the kāmāḥ here as viṣayāḥ, objects desired, and kāma-kāmī as one habitually desiring them.
It might render śānti as mere calm; Śaṅkara identifies it with mokṣa, liberation.
It might miss that the desires entering the sage do not disturb or control him; Śaṅkara says they dissolve in the self and do not make him subject to themselves.
It might flatten acala-pratiṣṭha into “immovable ocean”; Śaṅkara gives a bahuvrīhi-style analysis, “whose abiding/stability is unmoving.”
analyzer_disagreements: ByT5 gives āpūryamāṇam with lemma āp; I analyze it as the present passive participle āpūryamāṇa from ā-√pṝ, because Śaṅkara glosses it āpūryamāṇam adbhir, “being filled by waters.”
ByT5 segments acala + pratiṣṭham; I treat acala-pratiṣṭham as one bahuvrīhi compound, following Śaṅkara’s vigraha acalatayā pratiṣṭhā avasthitiḥ yasya tam acala-pratiṣṭham.
ByT5 gives finite-verb lemmas as praviś; per the requested format I give the bare root viś with prefix pra.
ByT5 segments kāma + kāmī; I treat kāma-kāmī as a single compound stem kāma-kāmin and construe its first member as the object desired, following Śaṅkara’s kāmyanta iti kāmāḥ viṣayāḥ.
open_questions: The commentary line as supplied reads “sa śāntir mokṣam āpnoti”; since the verse has śāntim and the context demands an object of āpnoti, this is probably unproofread for “sa śāntiṃ mokṣam āpnoti” or similar.
mula: āpūryamāṇam acala-pratiṣṭhaṃ samudram āpaḥ praviśanti yadvat | tadvat kāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntim āpnoti na kāma-kāmī
commentary_lines: āpūryamāṇam adbhir acala-pratiṣṭham acalatayā pratiṣṭhā avasthitiḥ yasya tam acala-pratiṣṭhaṃ samudram āpaḥ sarvato gatāḥ praviśanti svātmastham avikriyam eva santaṃ yadvat, tadvat kāmāḥ viṣaya-saṃnidhāv api sarvataḥ icchā-viśeṣāḥ yaṃ puruṣam --- samudram iva āpaḥ -- avikurvantaḥ praviśanti sarve ātmany eva pralīyante na svātma-vaśaṃ kurvanti, sa śāntir mokṣam āpnoti, netaraḥ kāma-kāmī, kāmyanta iti kāmāḥ viṣayāḥ tān kāmayituṃ śīlaṃ yasya saḥ kāma-kāmī, naiva prāpnotīty arthaḥ ||bhgs_2.70||
